clue.text: Arrived with something for sale in legendary court

blocks.note: came is a past tense of arrive
an item sold at auction is a lot

explanation.surface: Someone turns up at a fabled royal court carrying goods to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: Camelot is King Arthur's court in the Arthurian legends.

clue.text: Modest when holding power, act differently as one who doesn't

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word goes within another
doing something differently changes its order, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

blocks.note: coy means shy or modest
P is the physics symbol for power
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A shy performer is told to vary their act, unlike someone who never does.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the words before it: 'one who doesn't' means one who doesn't act differently, an imitator.
explanation.definitionFit: A copycat imitates others rather than doing anything original, so they never behave differently.

clue.text: Ruin study on current for electrical engineer

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil or ruin
to con is an old word for to study or learn
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A warning that poring over electrical current could wreck an engineer's career.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the study above the current.
explanation.definitionFit: Guglielmo Marconi was the Italian inventor and engineer who pioneered radio transmission.

clue.text: Sound clues for Northern city

indicators.note: the clue asks for what a word sounds like, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: leads are clues or hints, as in a police investigation

explanation.surface: A detective hunts for reliable hints pointing towards a city in the North.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeds is a large city in West Yorkshire in the north of England.

clue.text: Hard to swallow food requested – not a piece of cake

blocks.note: a tall story is one hard to believe or swallow
the dishes you ask for in a restaurant are your order

explanation.surface: A diner complains that the meal they asked for is unpleasant to eat, and certainly no dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The food words all belong to the surface: 'piece of cake' is the idiom for something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall order is a demanding task, the opposite of something easy, which a piece of cake is.

clue.text: Communicate incoherently, say, after second page

indicators.note: coming after means placed later, so the verb is written behind the two abbreviations

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
P is the abbreviation for page
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: Someone babbles nonsense after reaching the second page of a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like it introduces an example, but it is the verb that follows the two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: To sputter is to speak in hasty, spluttering bursts that make little sense.

clue.text: Cut made by censor ultimately disrupting cast

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept
something disrupting a group breaks into it, so it sits inside the other word

blocks.note: the final letter of censor
to cast off a skin is to shed it

explanation.surface: A censor's cut has upset the cast of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a group of actors, but here it is the verb meaning to throw off.
explanation.definitionFit: To shred is to cut or tear into thin strips.

clue.text: Admire run – scrambled single

indicators.note: scrambled things are mixed up, so the preceding letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket fan admires a single run that was hurriedly scrambled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' and 'run' suggest cricket scoring; single is the definition in its marital sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone single has no spouse, which is what unmarried means.

clue.text: Activate call for better service, part of multiple delivery

blocks.note: to trip a switch is to activate it
in tennis, let is called when a serve clips the net and must be taken again

explanation.surface: A tennis player triggers the umpire's call and gets to serve again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' sounds like more tennis or cricket, but it means a birth.
explanation.definitionFit: A triplet is one of three babies born in the same birth, a multiple delivery.

clue.text: Manipulate in lazy way, without flexibility

blocks.note: to rig an election is to manipulate it
doing something idly is doing it lazily

explanation.surface: Someone fixes a result lazily and stubbornly refuses to bend.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting rigidly means behaving in a stiff, unbending manner, with no give at all.

clue.text: English composer turned up with right instrument endlessly

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the next word is read backwards
without its end, the instrument's word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
R is the abbreviation for right
a cello is a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A composer arrives carrying the right instrument, which never stops playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived, but splits into an indicator and the word it reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Purcell was the leading English composer of the Baroque era, known for Dido and Aeneas.

clue.text: Striking a couple of males in scene of fighting

indicators.note: being in a place means sitting inside it, so these letters go within the venue word

blocks.note: taken as written
M for male, twice
a boxing ring is where fights take place

explanation.surface: Two men are landing blows on each other in a war zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple of males' suggests rams or men, but it is just two copies of the abbreviation for male.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramming is striking something hard and head-on, like a ram butting.

clue.text: What you're doing that's said to show irritation

blocks.note: first meaning: the puzzle the solver is working on right now
second meaning, read as two words: an angry remark

explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like a sound cue, but the second meaning is just a cross word, an irritated thing to say.
explanation.definitionFit: The solver is completing a puzzle grid, and split in two the answer is also an angry utterance.

clue.text: Gave judgment – regretted embracing panel's conclusion

indicators.note: embracing someone means wrapping arms round them, so one word encloses the letter
a conclusion is an ending, so the last letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: rued means regretted
the final letter of panel

explanation.surface: A judge delivered a verdict, then regretted what the panel concluded.
explanation.definitionFit: A court that has ruled has pronounced its formal decision on a case.

clue.text: Place in which she leaves this herd

indicators.note: when someone leaves a group they are no longer in it, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: the letters to be removed
the two words run together

explanation.surface: A cow wanders away from the herd she belonged to.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters sit across the two words; remove them and what remains is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Third is a placing in a race or contest, coming after first and second.

clue.text: Oldies act drunkenly, so put out of joint

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Some old folk behave drunkenly and end up injuring a shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislocate a bone is to force it out of its socket at a joint.

clue.text: Specialist medical subject involving oral examinations

definitions.text: Specialist medical subject involving oral examinations

blocks.note: surface reading: spoken tests, like a viva at university
setter's reading: examining people's mouths and teeth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Oral examinations' suggests a student's spoken test; the field in question examines the mouth itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the branch of medicine concerned with teeth and gums, where checkups look inside the mouth.

clue.text: Freshly minted coin in Pacific island

blocks.note: something freshly minted is brand new
a guinea was an old British gold coin worth 21 shillings

explanation.surface: A newly struck coin turns up on an island in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: A guinea is an old British coin, worth a pound and one shilling.
explanation.definitionFit: New Guinea is the large island north of Australia, shared by Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.

clue.text: Misrepresentation of stalwarts that's the final problem

indicators.note: a misrepresentation gives a distorted picture, so the letters appear in a different order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Loyal supporters are misrepresented, and that is the end of their patience.
explanation.definitionFit: The last straw is the final trouble that makes a situation unbearable, from the straw that broke the camel's back.

clue.text: Progressive revised bill covering historical period

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so the letters are rearranged
covering something means going all round it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
an era is a period of history

explanation.surface: A forward-looking politician amends a parliamentary bill that deals with history.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal and progressive both describe someone open to reform and new ideas.

clue.text: Like some old people having skill in bridge

indicators.note: being in something means lying inside it, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: art means skill or knack
a span is a bridge or arch across a gap

explanation.surface: Some pensioners are good at the card game bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' suggests the elderly and 'bridge' the card game; the people are the ancient Greeks of Sparta.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan describes the people of ancient Sparta, the Greek city-state famous for its warriors.

clue.text: Singular information in key source of notes about university

indicators.note: about means around, so the cash machine's letters surround the university

blocks.note: D is a musical key
a cash machine dispenses banknotes
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Unique facts about a university are found in the main source of lecture notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks musical beside 'key', but here it means banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Datum is the singular form of data, a single piece of information.

clue.text: British union's leader smothered in banal praise

indicators.note: the leader goes in front, so only the first letter of the word is kept
smothered in something means wholly covered by it, so these letters go inside the other word

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
the first letter of union
trite means banal or hackneyed

explanation.surface: A British trade union boss is buried under dull compliments.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribute is an expression of praise or admiration for someone.

clue.text: Record times

blocks.note: first meaning: the written record of a meeting
second meaning: short periods of time, sixty seconds each

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a stopwatch boast about record times; the words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutes are the official notes of a meeting, and also units of time measurement.

clue.text: Party vote with opposition?

blocks.note: first meaning: a lively celebration, informally
second meaning, read as three words: to cast a vote against

explanation.surface: A political party votes alongside the opposition in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: To vote with the opposition is to 'be a no'; run together those words make the answer. 'Party' is political only in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A beano is British slang for a noisy celebration or knees-up.

clue.text: Warning about small article is what produces results

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the warning word goes round the rest

blocks.note: a caution is a warning
S is the abbreviation for small
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A warning about a small item is what gets things done.
explanation.definitionFit: Causation is the process of cause and effect, by which actions bring about outcomes.

clue.text: Summit conference's opening before holiday

indicators.note: an opening is the start of something, so the first letter is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of conference
a rest is a break or holiday

explanation.surface: World leaders open their summit just before going on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summit conference' reads as a meeting of leaders; summit alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is the top or peak of a hill or wave, as is a summit.

clue.text: Examination that involves studying books

blocks.note: surface reading: a student revising textbooks for an exam
setter's reading: a company's account books checked by an accountant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Examination' and 'studying' paint a school scene, but the books are financial accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: An accountant's formal inspection of a firm's financial records is this kind of check.

clue.text: Fierce competition making artist copy, in a way

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is a standard tag for an artist
tracing is one way of copying a drawing

explanation.surface: Intense rivalry drives one painter to imitate another.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the relentless struggle for success in working life.

clue.text: Bound to upset, surely

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is certainly going to be offended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like the definition of certainty, but it is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions are adverbs of certainty, meaning without question.

clue.text: Like September of all months? Yes and no

definitions.text: Like September of all months? Yes and no

blocks.note: surface reading: is this month the biggest of all?
setter's reading: true of its name, which has the most letters, false of its thirty days

explanation.walkthrough: September's name has nine letters, more than any other month, but it has only thirty days, so the claim holds one way and fails the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of long describes whatever exceeds all others in length.

clue.text: What's central to smart lesson? That's simple

indicators.note: what is central lies in the middle, so the letters are found inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the middle of the two words

explanation.surface: A teacher asks what lies at the heart of a clever lesson, and declares it easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Artless means simple, natural and without guile or sophistication.
